title: Review—Measurement and Analysis of Cancer Biomarkers Based on Electrochemical Biosensors

subsections.subsection_title: Nanomaterials and Surface Engineering in Biosensor Design
subsections.content:
The design of high-performance electrochemical biosensors for cancer biomarker detection critically depends on the strategic integration of nanomaterials and advanced surface engineering techniques. Nanomaterials such as gold nanoparticles, carbon nanotubes, graphene derivatives, and metal-organic frameworks enhance electron transfer kinetics, increase electrode surface area, and facilitate immobilization of biorecognition elements with high density and orientation control. These properties collectively amplify signal transduction and lower detection limits, enabling the identification of low-abundance biomarkers in complex biological matrices. Surface engineering through self-assembled monolayers, polymer coatings, and bioorthogonal chemistries further improves biocompatibility, reduces non-specific adsorption, and stabilizes probe molecules on the transducer interface.

Recent advances have demonstrated the synergistic potential of nanomaterials in label-free impedimetric platforms, where nanostructured surfaces significantly enhance the sensitivity of impedance changes upon biomarker binding, as detailed in comprehensive reviews on nanomaterial-enabled signal amplification ref [5]. While fluorescence-based approaches like peptide microarray assays offer multiplexed profiling of proteolytic activities, their principles inform surface functionalization strategies for electrochemical sensors, particularly in designing selective capture layers ref [1]. The convergence of nanomaterial architecture and surface chemistry continues to drive innovation in next-generation biosensors for point-of-care cancer diagnostics.

Cancer biomarkers detected via electrochemical biosensors span a diverse array of molecular species, including proteins, nucleic acids, and glycoconjugates, each offering unique advantages for early diagnosis and monitoring. MicroRNAs (miRNAs), such as miR-21, miR-155, and miR-335, have emerged as highly promising circulating biomarkers for breast cancer, with multiplexed profiles demonstrating superior sensitivity and specificity compared to single miRNA detection ref [3]. Similarly, glycosylation alterations on serum glycoproteins serve as sensitive indicators of malignant transformation, with label-free electrochemical lectin-based biosensors enabling glycoprofiling of cancer-associated glycans without requiring fluorescent or enzymatic labels ref [7]. Protein biomarkers remain central to electrochemical detection; for instance, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) in liver cancer has been quantified using bienzyme-functionalized silica nanobeads in a conductometric immunoassay, achieving sub-pg/mL detection limits ref [8]. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) has been targeted using TCNQ-doped Cu-MOF platforms, leveraging enhanced electron transfer for improved signal amplification ref [7]. In bladder cancer, apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1) has been successfully detected using bottom-up assembled silicon nanowire conductometric sensors, enabling label-free, real-time monitoring in physiological samples ref [8]. Additionally, the pleural mesothelioma biomarker HAPLN1 has been selectively captured using molecularly imprinted electrochemical surfaces, demonstrating the feasibility of imprinting for rare tumor antigens ref [4].

The versatility of electrochemical platforms allows for the detection of both abundant and low-abundance biomarkers across diverse biofluids, including serum, urine, and pleural fluid. Emerging trends emphasize multiplexed detection, point-of-care compatibility, and the integration of nanomaterials to enhance sensitivity. The convergence of biomarker biology with advanced transduction strategies continues to expand the clinical utility of electrochemical biosensors in precision oncology.

subsections.subsection_title: Electrochemical Sensing Platforms for Biomarker Analysis
subsections.content:
Electrochemical sensing platforms for cancer biomarker analysis have evolved significantly through the integration of advanced electrode architectures and label-free detection strategies. Screen-printed gold electrodes, when functionalized with polymer-coated magnetic microparticles, enable ultrasensitive detection of inflammatory biomarkers like TNF-α in complex matrices such as artificial saliva, demonstrating clinical translatability for non-invasive diagnostics ref [10]. Similarly, microelectrode arrays have been employed for label-free electrical detection of exosomal microRNAs via semiconductor-based potentiometry, offering high-throughput, multiplexed profiling of circulating miRNAs as minimally invasive cancer indicators ref [13]. For glycoprofiling of protein biomarkers, chronopotentiometric stripping with mercury electrodes has enabled reagent-free discrimination of sialylated isoforms of PSA through specific lectin binding, providing insights into cancer-associated glycosylation changes ref [16]. Surface 3D microarrays modified with benzoboric acid have enhanced capture efficiency of circulating tumor cells by exploiting sialic acid interactions, while enabling gentle cell recovery for downstream analysis ref [9].

Bioimpedimetric platforms have emerged as powerful tools for differentiating cancer cell aggressiveness by correlating real-time impedance dynamics with proliferation and death resistance phenotypes, as demonstrated in MCF-7 and MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cell lines ref [11]. Label-free impedance cytosensors functionalized with mannosyl ligands have achieved high specificity for MDA-MB-231 cells by targeting overexpressed mannose receptors, offering a promising alternative to antibody-based capture ref [12]. Capacitive aptasensors based on interdigitated gold electrodes have enabled detection of HER2 in undiluted human serum with sub-picomolar sensitivity, circumventing sample dilution and preserving physiological relevance ref [13]. The convergence of miniaturized nanobiosensors with microfluidic systems is further shifting diagnostic paradigms by enabling integrated sample processing, multiplexed detection, and point-of-care deployment in clinically relevant samples ref [14].

subsections.subsection_title: Exosome-Based Electrochemical Biosensing for Liquid Biopsy
subsections.content:
Exosome-based electrochemical biosensing has emerged as a powerful strategy for liquid biopsy, enabling non-invasive, sensitive, and rapid detection of cancer-derived exosomes in bodily fluids. These nanoscale vesicles carry molecular cargo—including proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids—that reflect the phenotypic state of their parent tumor cells, making them ideal biomarkers for early cancer diagnosis and monitoring. Recent advances have leveraged electrochemical transduction coupled with specific biorecognition elements, such as antibodies or aptamers, to achieve high selectivity and low detection limits. Integrated magneto-electrochemical platforms, for instance, combine magnetic enrichment with enzymatic signal amplification to enable multiplexed protein profiling of exosomes in clinical plasma samples within an hour, significantly outperforming conventional methods in speed and sensitivity ref [5].

Furthermore, concentration-normalized electroanalytical assays have been developed to account for variable exosome yields across samples, enhancing quantitative reliability by normalizing signal output to exosome count rather than volume ref [6]. These approaches are often integrated with nanomaterials such as graphene or gold nanoparticles to enhance electron transfer and surface area, improving signal-to-noise ratios. Recent reviews highlight the growing diversity of electrochemical biosensor designs, including impedance, amperometric, and voltammetric formats, each tailored to detect specific exosomal markers like EpCAM, CD63, or HER2 ref [17]. The field is also advancing toward point-of-care applications through miniaturization and portable device integration, as emphasized in comprehensive surveys on exosomal protein detection via liquid biopsy ref [19].

subsections.subsection_title: Protein Biomarkers Detected by Electrochemical Immunosensors
subsections.content:
Electrochemical immunosensors have emerged as powerful tools for the sensitive and selective detection of cancer-associated protein biomarkers in complex biological matrices. Sandwich-type configurations, leveraging primary and secondary antibody binding coupled with electroactive labels, have demonstrated exceptional performance in quantifying carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), a widely studied tumor marker. For instance, a sandwich immunosensor utilizing Ag/MoS₂@Fe₃O₄ nanocomposites achieved high sensitivity for CEA detection, while an alternative design integrated ferrocene derivatives as internal redox reporters, enabling reliable quantification in human serum with a detection limit as low as 0.01 ng mL⁻¹ ref [21], ref [22]. Label-free approaches have also gained traction, such as the use of gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) and poly-o-aminophenol films to enhance signal transduction and reduce nonspecific binding, enabling impedimetric detection of CEA without enzymatic labels ref [23].

Beyond CEA, electrochemical immunosensors have been successfully applied to other clinically relevant protein targets. Matrix metalloproteinase-3 (MMP-3), a key mediator of tumor invasion, was detected at sub-picomolar levels using vertically aligned single-wall carbon nanotube (SWCNT) arrays with enzyme-labeled secondary antibodies ref [24]. Similarly, interleukin-6 (IL-6), an inflammatory cytokine linked to tumor progression, was measured with detection limits as low as 10 pg mL⁻¹ using glutathione-protected AuNPs, outperforming SWCNT forests in dynamic range ref [25]. The detection of CD147/EMMPRIN on cancer cell surfaces has also been achieved through HRP-amplified electrochemical readouts enhanced by gold nanoparticles, enabling quantification at the single-cell level ref [8]. Furthermore, label-free impedimetric sensors for murine double minute 2 (MDM2) in brain tissue achieved ultralow detection limits of 0.29 pg mL⁻¹ using cysteamine-monolayer-modified electrodes and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy ref [9].

Recent reviews highlight the critical role of nanomaterial-assisted signal amplification strategies—such as noble metal nanoparticles, carbon nanotubes, and 2D materials—in pushing detection limits to femtogram levels, thereby enabling early cancer diagnosis from minimal sample volumes ref [27]. These platforms are increasingly being optimized for point-of-care applications through miniaturization, multiplexing, and integration with microfluidics, establishing electrochemical immunosensors as indispensable tools in precision oncology.

subsections.subsection_title: Nucleic Acid Biomarkers: ctDNA, miRNA, and Methylation Analysis
subsections.content:
Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has emerged as a pivotal nucleic acid biomarker for noninvasive cancer diagnostics, offering real-time insights into tumor mutational profiles. Recent electrochemical biosensors have enabled ultrasensitive detection of ctDNA mutations without enzymatic amplification, as demonstrated by the electrochemical clamp assay that selectively captures mutant sequences in serum within 15 minutes, bypassing PCR-related biases ref [32]. Advances in nanomaterials have further enhanced sensitivity; for instance, a nitrogen-doped graphene aerogel/gold nanostar platform achieved low-femtomolar detection of cfDNA in human serum by amplifying electron transfer kinetics ref [30]. These platforms are particularly valuable for identifying low-abundance variants in early-stage cancers, where ctDNA concentrations are minimal.

MicroRNA (miRNA) biomarkers, such as miR-141 and miR-155, are increasingly targeted due to their regulatory roles in tumorigenesis and stability in biofluids. Label-free electrochemical biosensors have been developed to detect miRNAs directly in serum, eliminating the need for labeling or amplification. A conducting polymer nanostructured with carbon nanotubes enabled reagentless detection of miR-141 in prostate cancer samples, leveraging the conductive properties of the hybrid matrix for direct signal transduction ref [8]. Similarly, a Pd nanoparticle-enhanced multilayer biosensor achieved a detection limit of 1.87 pM for miR-155 by improving electron transfer and target immobilization ref [9].

Epigenetic alterations, particularly DNA methylation, offer another layer of specificity for cancer detection. An electrochemical method based on paired-end tagging and amplification has been developed to accurately quantify methylated ctDNA from clinical plasma, enabling high-specificity discrimination between methylated and unmethylated alleles ref [31]. These approaches, combined with nanomaterial-enhanced electrode surfaces, are paving the way for multiplexed, point-of-care liquid biopsy platforms that integrate ctDNA, miRNA, and methylation analysis into a single diagnostic framework.

subsections.subsection_title: Redox and Metabolic Biomarkers: Glutathione, Hypoxia, and Cellular Microenvironment Sensing
subsections.content:
Redox and metabolic biomarkers, particularly reduced glutathione (GSH), play pivotal roles in cancer progression by modulating oxidative stress and cellular redox homeostasis. Electrochemical biosensors for GSH detection have advanced significantly through the use of chemically modified carbon-based electrodes, including glassy carbon, carbon paste, and screen-printed platforms, which enhance sensitivity and selectivity via tailored surface modifications and electrocatalytic materials ref [36]. Recent innovations in nanostructure-based sensors, such as ZnO/CNTs composites and graphene hybrids, have further improved detection limits to the nanomolar range, enabling reliable quantification in complex biological matrices like serum ref [37]. A comprehensive review of electrochemical GSH sensing from 2012–2018 highlights progress in electrode design, signal amplification, and in-vivo applicability, underscoring the shift toward minimally invasive, high-throughput clinical diagnostics ref [39].

Beyond GSH, tumor hypoxia—a hallmark of aggressive cancers—has become a critical target for electrochemical sensing due to its role in metastasis, therapy resistance, and metabolic reprogramming. The METOXIA consortium has pioneered integrated biosensing strategies that bridge hypoxia biology with microsensor technology, enabling real-time monitoring of oxygen gradients in tumor microenvironments ref [8]. Complementary to this, microfabricated systems such as the Sensing Cell Culture Flask (SCCF) integrate amperometric oxygen and potentiometric pH sensors directly into standard cell culture flasks, allowing non-invasive, longitudinal monitoring of cellular respiration and acidification in real time under physiologically relevant conditions ref [9]. Similarly, transparent microfluidic multi-sensor platforms enable simultaneous detection of oxygen, pH, and metabolites in 2D and 3D cancer models, facilitating high-content drug screening and personalized oncology applications ref [10].

subsections.subsection_title: Cancer Cell Detection and Enumeration via Electrochemical Interfaces
subsections.content:
Electrochemical interfaces have emerged as powerful platforms for the direct detection and enumeration of cancer cells, leveraging specific biorecognition elements and signal amplification strategies to achieve high sensitivity in complex biological matrices. Label-free aptasensors constructed via layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly, such as those incorporating ferrocene-functionalized graphene nanocomposites and the AS1411 aptamer, enable selective capture of cancer cells through G-quadruplex binding, with impedance changes due to the insulating cell membrane providing a measurable signal down to 10 cells/mL ref [41]. Integration of immunosensing with microfluidic cell adhesion technologies on patterned ITO electrodes allows for scalable, rapid enumeration of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) with precise spatial control and minimal sample volume ref [42]. Recent advances have extended beyond surface binding to 3D microenvironments, where electric cell/matrigel-substrate impedance sensing (3D-ECMIS) enables real-time, label-free monitoring of cell viability and drug response in physiologically relevant scaffolds, correlating impedance magnitude with cell density ref [44].

Further innovation has been achieved through DNA-based signal amplification, such as rolling circle amplification (RCA) coupled with EpCAM-targeted magnetic nanospheres, which capture CTCs and generate electrochemical currents via DNA-molybdate redox reactions, achieving ultrasensitive detection in spiked blood samples ref [7]. Three-dimensional graphene biointerfaces have demonstrated single-cell sensitivity by enhancing electron transfer kinetics and increasing surface area for cell adhesion, enabling real-time monitoring of individual cancer cell dynamics ref [8]. These approaches are complemented by comprehensive reviews that contextualize the biological and engineering challenges in CTC detection, emphasizing the need for high recovery efficiency, minimal cell damage, and real-time quantification for clinical translation ref [45]. Collectively, these electrochemical strategies are shifting the paradigm from bulk analysis to single-cell resolution, paving the way for precision oncology applications.

subsections.subsection_title: Microfluidic Electrochemical Platforms for Multiplexed and Point-of-Care Cancer Diagnostics
subsections.content:
Microfluidic electrochemical platforms have emerged as powerful tools for multiplexed and point-of-care (POC) cancer diagnostics, enabling rapid, sensitive, and simultaneous detection of multiple biomarkers from minimal sample volumes. These platforms integrate microfluidic handling with electrochemical transduction to automate assay workflows, reduce reagent consumption, and enhance reproducibility. A notable example is the disposable electrochemical microfluidic chip developed for early gastric cancer diagnosis, which concurrently quantifies six biomarkers—including CEA, CA19-9, and P53—with sensitivity surpassing conventional ELISA, while minimizing cross-contamination through a custom three-electrode design ref [47]. Similarly, high-throughput electrochemical microfluidic immunoarrays have been engineered to detect multiple cancer protein biomarkers in a single run, leveraging spatially resolved electrode arrays for parallelized immunoassays and enabling scalable screening ref [4].

Beyond static diagnostics, automated microfluidic systems now facilitate real-time, continuous monitoring of cell-secreted biomarkers in dynamic biological environments. An integrated bead-based electrochemical immunosensor combined with a microfluidic bioreactor enables long-term, in-line quantification of hepatocyte-secreted proteins such as transferrin and albumin during hepatotoxicity studies, demonstrating feasibility for monitoring tumor microenvironment dynamics ref [5]. These innovations highlight a paradigm shift from single-point assays to dynamic, closed-loop diagnostic systems. Further advancements include on-chip sample preparation, integrated sample-to-answer workflows, and compatibility with portable readout devices, positioning microfluidic electrochemical platforms as ideal candidates for decentralized cancer screening in resource-limited settings. The convergence of multiplexing, automation, and miniaturization is accelerating the translation of these technologies into clinical POC applications.

subsections.subsection_title: Advanced Transduction Techniques and Signal Amplification Strategies
subsections.content:
Advanced transduction techniques in electrochemical biosensors have evolved beyond conventional amperometric and potentiometric methods to include sophisticated impedance-based strategies that enable label-free, real-time monitoring of cancer biomarkers. Faradaic and non-faradaic electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) offer complementary advantages: faradaic EIS provides higher sensitivity through redox mediator involvement, while non-faradaic EIS enables miniaturization and compatibility with point-of-care platforms by eliminating the need for redox couples, making it ideal for clinical deployment ref [49]. To overcome inherent sensitivity limitations, cascaded signal amplification strategies have been introduced, such as Ca²⁺-triggered pH-responsive sodium alginate hydrogel precipitation, which leverages the dual action of gold nanoparticle-CaCO₃ microspheres to induce steric hindrance and subsequent hydrogel formation, resulting in ultralow detection limits down to 0.09 fg mL⁻¹ for prostate-specific antigen ref [52].

Further innovation has emerged through enzyme-mimetic cascade catalysis, exemplified by Cu-MOF nanoparticles coupled with glucose oxidase to initiate radical polymerization of N-isopropylacrylamide, generating a conductive-insulating poly(NIPAM) layer that dramatically amplifies impedance signals for carbohydrate antigen 15-3 detection with a limit of 5.06 μU/mL ref [5]. In parallel, ratiometric DNA-based transduction strategies, such as metallization-mediated hybridization chain reactions, enable intracellular redox homeostasis monitoring by converting subtle redox changes into quantifiable electrochemical ratios, facilitating cancer cell discrimination without labels ref [6]. These approaches collectively represent a paradigm shift toward multi-stage signal amplification, integrating chemical, enzymatic, and nanomaterial-driven mechanisms to achieve unprecedented sensitivity and specificity in cancer biomarker detection.

subsections.subsection_title: Electrochemical Immunosensors and Affinity-Based Detection Strategies
subsections.content:
Electrochemical immunosensors represent a cornerstone in the detection of cancer protein biomarkers, leveraging the high specificity of antibody-antigen interactions coupled with the sensitivity and simplicity of electrochemical transduction. These platforms enable the quantification of clinically relevant markers such as PSA, CEA, CA-125, and CA 15-3 directly in complex biological fluids, facilitating early diagnosis and therapeutic monitoring. Recent advances have focused on enhancing signal transduction through optimized electrode interfaces and novel immobilization strategies, with particular emphasis on minimizing non-specific binding and improving reproducibility in point-of-care settings. Ref [1] provides a comprehensive overview of electrochemical immunosensors targeting key cancer proteins, highlighting their clinical utility and the necessity of multi-biomarker panels to overcome the limitations of single-marker assays.

Signal amplification in electrochemical ELISA-based formats has significantly lowered detection limits, enabling identification of biomarkers at femtomolar concentrations. Ref [2] details recent innovations in enzyme-labeled immunoassays, including nanomaterial-enhanced horseradish peroxidase systems and catalytic nanotags that amplify redox currents. Furthermore, molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs) have emerged as synthetic alternatives to antibodies, offering robustness and reusability; ref [55] demonstrates the first use of poly(Toluidine Blue)-based MIPs for the selective detection of CA 15-3 in disposable sensors, achieving high specificity without biological recognition elements. The transition from laboratory prototypes to clinically validated devices remains a critical challenge, as emphasized in ref [7], which reviews electrochemical immunosensors validated with real patient samples and underscores the importance of correlating sensor performance with established clinical thresholds and diagnostic outcomes.

subsections.subsection_title: Nanomaterial-Enhanced Electrochemical Biosensors for Cancer Biomarker Detection
subsections.content:
Nanomaterial-enhanced electrochemical biosensors have revolutionized the detection of cancer biomarkers by leveraging the unique physicochemical properties of nanoscale materials to achieve unprecedented sensitivity and selectivity. Metal nanoparticles, carbon nanotubes, and graphene-based materials are widely employed to increase electrode surface area, facilitate electron transfer, and enable high-density immobilization of biorecognition elements such as antibodies and aptamers. These nanomaterials not only enhance signal transduction but also serve as catalytic labels or redox mediators, significantly amplifying electrochemical responses. For instance, the integration of graphene and its derivatives with electroactive nanocomposites has enabled ultrasensitive detection of protein biomarkers at femtomolar levels, as demonstrated in recent studies ref [6]. Moreover, the use of 2D nanomaterials such as transition metal dichalcogenides and boron nitride has expanded the scope of multiplexed detection by providing tunable surface chemistry and excellent stability in biological matrices ref [6].

Signal amplification strategies have been further advanced through the design of hybrid nanomaterials, such as polyaniline-Au/Pd composites, which offer distinct redox potentials for simultaneous multiplexed immunoassays of multiple tumor markers including CEA, CA199, and AFP ref [8]. These materials enable differential signal resolution in a single assay, critical for accurate cancer subtyping. Nanomaterial-assisted strategies have also been pivotal in low-abundance biomarker detection, with studies reporting detection limits orders of magnitude lower than conventional methods ref [57]. Comprehensive reviews highlight the systematic application of nanomaterials in both labeled and label-free immunosensors, emphasizing their role in improving linear range, reproducibility, and clinical applicability ref [58]. The convergence of nanotechnology with electrochemical transduction has thus established a robust platform for next-generation cancer diagnostics, particularly in point-of-care settings where rapid, low-cost, and multiplexed analysis is paramount ref [59].

subsections.subsection_title: DNA and Aptamer-Based Electrochemical Biosensors for Genetic and Epigenetic Cancer Markers
subsections.content:
DNA- and aptamer-based electrochemical biosensors have emerged as powerful tools for the detection of genetic and epigenetic cancer markers, offering high specificity, sensitivity, and compatibility with point-of-care platforms. DNA biosensors exploit sequence-specific hybridization to detect mutations, single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), and gene expression alterations associated with carcinogenesis, as demonstrated in the detection of BRCA1 mutations using antifouling peptide monolayers that minimize nonspecific adsorption in complex biological fluids ref [62]. Meanwhile, aptamers—single-stranded nucleic acids with tailored 3D conformations—provide superior binding affinity for targets such as methylated DNA, oncogenic miRNAs, and epigenetic modifiers, enabling label-free and amplification-free detection strategies ref [66]. Recent advances integrate rolling circle amplification (RCA) with electrochemical readouts to achieve ultralow detection limits for DNA methylation, as shown in tetrahedron-structured RCA systems that exponentially amplify signal from trace methylated sequences ref [11]. These platforms are further enhanced by nanomaterials and microfluidic integration, facilitating multiplexed analysis of both genetic mutations and epigenetic signatures from minimal clinical samples ref [10]. The versatility of aptamers in recognizing non-protein targets, including small molecules and modified nucleotides, positions them as indispensable alternatives to antibodies in next-generation liquid biopsy assays ref [7].

The foundational principles of DNA biosensors for cancer diagnosis, including hybridization kinetics and signal transduction mechanisms, have been systematically reviewed to guide sensor design for clinical translation ref [61]. Combined with innovations in self-assembled monolayers and isothermal amplification, these biosensors now enable early detection of cancer-associated epigenetic alterations such as promoter hypermethylation in circulating tumor DNA. Ongoing challenges include improving stability in serum, reducing background noise, and standardizing SELEX protocols for aptamer selection, yet their potential for multiplexed, low-cost, and rapid diagnostics continues to drive significant research investment ref [66].

Figures and tables in electrochemical biosensor studies for cancer biomarkers serve critical roles in visualizing signal transduction mechanisms, sensor architectures, and quantitative performance metrics. Well-designed figures often illustrate the integration of nanomaterials, electrode modifications, and microfluidic components, enabling readers to grasp complex sensing interfaces at a glance. For instance, schematic diagrams of tetrahedral DNA nanostructures coupled with rolling circle amplification have been instrumental in clarifying signal amplification pathways in methylation detection [1]. Tables summarizing limit of detection (LOD), linear range, selectivity, and clinical sample validation across studies allow direct comparison of sensor performance, as demonstrated in multiplexed protein biomarker arrays [2]. The use of color-coded impedance spectra and voltammograms in recent publications enhances interpretability of faradaic and non-faradaic responses [3]. Moreover, graphical abstracts in high-impact journals increasingly synthesize sensor design, target analyte, and clinical relevance into single illustrative panels, improving dissemination [4].

Standardization of figure presentation remains inconsistent, with some studies omitting scale bars, error margins, or control comparisons, limiting reproducibility. Recent efforts advocate for standardized reporting templates, particularly for electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) Nyquist plots and amperometric calibration curves [5]. The inclusion of real-sample validation data in figures—such as serum or plasma spiked with biomarkers—adds clinical translational weight [6]. Furthermore, 3D renderings of microelectrode arrays and microfluidic channels have become essential for conveying spatial sensing configurations [7]. Comparative tables of nanomaterials (e.g., graphene, AuNPs, MOFs) and their associated signal enhancements are increasingly used to guide material selection [8]. The strategic use of heatmaps to represent multiplexed biomarker profiles from patient cohorts has emerged as a powerful tool for diagnostic pattern recognition [9].

subsections.subsection_title: Early Detection of Cancer Biomarkers via Electrochemical Biosensors
subsections.content:
Electrochemical biosensors have emerged as powerful tools for the early detection of cancer biomarkers, offering high sensitivity, rapid response, and compatibility with point-of-care applications. Recent advances have enabled the detection of low-concentration tumor markers in complex biological fluids such as serum and plasma, facilitating non-invasive liquid biopsy strategies. For instance, ref [67] provides a comprehensive review of electrochemical immuno-, geno-, and aptasensors for early-stage breast cancer screening, highlighting the utility of biomarkers like CA 15-3, HER2, and circulating tumor DNA. The integration of aptamers and DNA-based probes has further enhanced specificity, allowing discrimination of single-nucleotide polymorphisms associated with oncogenic mutations. Additionally, label-free impedimetric and voltammetric platforms have been successfully applied to detect exosomal proteins and microRNAs linked to early tumorigenesis, as demonstrated in studies targeting miR-21 and CD63 ref [41]. The development of multiplexed electrochemical microarrays has enabled simultaneous profiling of multiple biomarkers, improving diagnostic accuracy and reducing false positives ref [21]. These systems are increasingly being miniaturized and integrated with microfluidics to enable automated, high-throughput screening in clinical settings.

Despite progress, challenges remain in standardizing sample preparation, minimizing matrix effects in undiluted biofluids, and ensuring reproducibility across diverse patient cohorts. Emerging strategies incorporating molecularly imprinted polymers and nanomaterial-enhanced interfaces are addressing these limitations, as seen in the use of poly(Toluidine Blue) for CA 15-3 detection ref [41] and graphene-based electrodes for cfDNA quantification. Future efforts must focus on clinical validation in large-scale cohorts and regulatory approval pathways to transition these technologies from research labs to routine oncology practice.

subsections.subsection_title: Nanomaterial-Enhanced Signal Strategies for Low-Abundance Biomarker Detection
subsections.content:
The detection of low-abundance cancer biomarkers remains a critical challenge in early diagnosis, where nanomaterial-enhanced signal amplification strategies have emerged as pivotal enablers of ultrasensitive electrochemical biosensing. Nanomaterials such as gold nanoparticles, graphene derivatives, metal-organic frameworks, and carbon nanotubes significantly enhance electron transfer kinetics, increase surface area for biomolecule immobilization, and facilitate catalytic signal amplification. For instance, the integration of nanomaterial-assisted signal enhancement in electrochemical affinity biosensors has enabled detection limits in the femtomolar range for tumor protein markers like CA15-3 and CEA, as demonstrated by Farzin and Shamsipur ref [25]. Recent innovations include the use of Pd nanoparticles as both signal enhancers and molecular linkers in microRNA biosensors, improving sensitivity through synergistic catalytic effects ref [22]. Additionally, nitrogen-doped graphene aerogels coupled with gold nanostars have been employed for the direct detection of circulating free DNA in serum, leveraging their high conductivity and biocompatibility ref [54]. The development of 3D graphene biointerfaces has further enabled single-cell-level monitoring by maximizing biomarker capture efficiency and minimizing non-specific binding ref [66].

Beyond conventional nanomaterials, hybrid architectures combining magnetic nanoparticles with redox-active polymers have enabled efficient sample preconcentration and signal amplification in complex biological matrices. Such strategies are particularly effective in point-of-care applications where sample volume and purity are limited. The use of Cu-metal organic frameworks doped with TCNQ has also shown promise in conductometric immunosensing of prostate-specific antigen, offering high selectivity and low background noise ref [65]. Collectively, these advances underscore the transformative role of nanomaterial design in overcoming the sensitivity barriers inherent in detecting trace-level cancer biomarkers, paving the way for clinically viable early detection platforms.
